full_text: Global tech stocks plunge as US midterms add to AI slowdown fears Investors have reacted to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the AI industry. Hundreds of billions of dollars in market value has been wiped from major tech firms in the US and Asia in a stock market rout after the US midterm elections sparked concerns of a slowdown in artificial intelligence development. Shares in firms across the tech and AI sectors plummeted following Democratic wins after election campaigns run on slowing AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite index closed down by more than 5.5%, losing an estimated $2.5tn (£1.9tn) in market value, according to Dow Jones data, while other key US stock indexes also saw big losses in their worst days since 2025. The sell-off comes on top of broader concerns about whether the huge amounts being spent on AI will pay off. In Asia, tech-heavy indexes fell sharply on Friday morning as firms that make the computer chips and other equipment that power AI saw their shares slide. The Nikkei 225 in Japan was 6% lower in early trading as shares in memory chip maker Kioxia lost over 12.6% and rival Tokyo Electron slipped by 9.5%. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix fell by more than 11.5%, while Samsung was down by nearly 10%. The sell-off in Seoul sent the Kospi index plunging more than 8.5%, triggering a so-called circuit breaker, a mechanism that temporarily halts trading to curb panic selling. Taiwan's Taiex dropped by more than 8.3%, with chipmaking giant TSMC falling by nearly 8.5%. It marks a "continuation of worries" over the level of spending on AI infrastructure, said MarketWatch chips analyst Britney Nguyen.

full_text: Armani heirs have no plans to sell fashion house to major companies — Reuters The heirs intend to distribute a minority stake among several investors, thereby preventing the emergence of a dominant shareholder LONDON, November 5. /TASS/. The heirs of the late Italian fashion designer Giorgio Armani, who control the fashion house bearing his name, have no plans to sell it to major brands and instead intend to retain control of the company through a stock market listing,Reutersreported, citing sources. According to the report, the designer’s heirs favor listing Giorgio Armani shares on a stock exchange rather than selling the company to a major industry player. Unlike earlier scenarios that envisaged transferring control to a single buyer, the heirs now intend to distribute a minority stake among several investors, thereby preventing the emergence of a dominant shareholder. The leading contenders for stakes in the company are French cosmetics giant L’Oreal and Franco-Italian eyewear group EssilorLuxottica. Giorgio Armani, the founder of the fashion house, died in September last year at the age of 91. His will stipulated that 15% of the company’s shares be sold within 18 months of his death. If, after fulfilling this requirement, the family decides against transferring the remaining controlling interest to a single strategic investor, the will mandates a public listing of the company’s shares within three to eight years of the founder’s death.

Lake Powell, the second-largest human-made reservoir in the US, has lost nearly 7% of its potential storage capacity since 1963, when Glen Canyon Dam was built, a new report shows. In addition to water loss due to anintense multiyear drought, the US Geological Survey and the Bureau of Reclamationreport found, Lake Powell faced an average annual loss in storage capacity of about 33,270 acre-feet, or 11 billion gallons, per year between 1963 and 2018. That’s enough water to fill the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall about 1,600 times.
